competitors.name: Hygiene Technologies International (HygieneTech)
competitors.what_they_do: Torrance-based industrial hygiene firm that Farmers uses as its approved smoke/contamination assessor. It is the incumbent carrier-side assessor and the target of the Ghazarian v. Fire Insurance Exchange class action (LA Superior Court, Feb 2026), which alleges its inspections missed industry standards and understated contamination. I did not verify the firm's own website, so the URL is the news report.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Private, no funding data found. Named in two Singleton Schreiber class actions against carrier-retained hygiene vendors (see also law.com/therecorder, 2026-02-27).

competitors.name: Rimkus
competitors.what_they_do: Forensic engineering and consulting firm. Its CIHs do smoke, soot and contamination analysis for insurers, adjusters and carrier-side law firms on the Eaton and Palisades fires and earlier ones. Sells 'defensible methodology' built on AIHA guidance.
competitors.scale_or_funding: 70+ US offices, 900+ credentialed experts. Established private firm.

competitors.name: Safeguard EnviroGroup (Brad Kovar)
competitors.what_they_do: Environmental consultancy specializing in wildfire smoke assessment. Its founder published a 'Defensible Framework for Post-Wildfire Smoke Damage Claims' in Claims Journal (Aug 2026), aimed at carriers and built on AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI and ASTM. This is already the 'defensible protocol for carriers' pitch.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Small private consultancy, no funding data found.

competitors.name: EHS Analytical Solutions
competitors.what_they_do: CIH-led fire and smoke assessments across California: surface sampling, VOC and particulate air testing, HVAC evaluation, post-remediation verification and clearance testing. Uses partner fire-forensics labs. Turnaround is 1-5 business days. No published protocol, software or carrier compliance product.

competitors.name: Home BioTesting
competitors.what_they_do: Southern California char/soot/ash, lead and asbestos sampling with reports and insurance-claim documentation support. Claims 9 years working with major insurers and 24-hour response.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Small private firm. No funding data found.

competitors.name: Vert Environmental and other regional smoke-testing shops
competitors.what_they_do: Soot, ash and char residue testing for restoration claims. One of many small firms (also Purified Environments, Guaranteed Property and Mold Inspection, Environmental Consulting Industries) selling clearance reports and certificates today. That covers the 'smoke clearance certificate' and per-home assessment revenue lines.

competitors.name: IICRC / RIA / CIRI Technical Guide for Wildfire Restoration (V2, Dec 2025) and ANSI/IICRC S700
competitors.what_they_do: Published industry guidance and standard that the idea proposes to build on. It is not a service. It means a citable, consensus wildfire protocol already exists and the 'interim protocol' would sit on top of it. I could not read the PDF, so its exact sampling content is unverified.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Industry standards bodies. S700 is under revision.

competitors.name: AIHA Technical Guide for Wildfire Impact Assessments (2nd ed.)
competitors.what_they_do: The IH profession's reference for sampling in wildfire-impacted buildings. It recommends multiple locations near and far from entry points, plus attics, garages and exteriors. Won the AIHA 2025 Critics' Choice Award and is what carrier-side firms cite.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Professional association publication, sold through the AIHA marketplace.

competitors.name: Purdue Center for Plumbing Safety (Whelton/Bollens): 'After the Wildfire: Building Environmental Testing'
competitors.what_they_do: Free public guidance (Sept 2025) telling owners and health officials what to sample, and a free independent review of homeowners' test reports. Reportedly finds improper methods and wrong comparison standards. Whelton also gave opinions to the CDI task force. EFRU points residents to it instead of publishing its own protocol.

competitors.name: Eaton Fire Residents United (EFRU) data maps
competitors.what_they_do: Advocacy group that crowdsources professional test reports into pre- and post-remediation contamination maps. Its data and pressure helped drive AB 1642 and AB 1795. It holds the largest open field dataset, which is the 'most field data' moat the idea wants. It does not sell testing.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Volunteer coalition, roughly 50-80 homes of shared data reported.

competitors.name: Sedgwick and other carrier TPAs
competitors.what_they_do: Large claims TPAs that would be the buyers or gatekeepers for a carrier compliance dashboard. Already used for CAT surge capacity and digital claim tooling. I found no smoke-IH product, so this is an adjacent feature risk rather than a proven competitor.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Sedgwick is a leading TPA. Program business alone exceeds $5B in gross written premium.

competitors.name: State of California (CalEPA / DTSC / CDI)
competitors.what_they_do: DTSC must adopt lead and asbestos standards by 12/31/2028 and other contaminants by 12/31/2029, with ARB indoor-air guidance by 12/31/2028. The April 2026 draft of AB 1795 also had CalEPA and CDI build training and certification programs for IHs, restoration contractors, labs and adjusters by 1/1/2028. It let local health agencies issue binding interim sampling standards. I could not confirm which of those survived in the chaptered bill.
competitors.scale_or_funding: Government. Will write the eventual standard and may certify the people who do the work.

white_space:
Mostly assessment supply and free guidance are crowded, so the raw 'do smoke testing' and 'publish a protocol' layers are not white space. Dozens of CIH-led firms sell $2k-$4k+ assessments and clearance certificates. AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI, Purdue and EFRU already publish free or cheap protocols. Safeguard EnviroGroup is already pitching a 'defensible framework' to carriers. State agencies (AB 1795 drafts) planned to certify IHs, contractors and labs, which undercuts the training-fee line.

Still unserved: (1) Carrier and TPA operations under AB 1795. Nobody offers a claim-level compliance layer with the 30-day inspection clock, an audit-ready sampling plan mapped to zones, chain-of-custody records and an evidence file, sold as software. Carriers are 'technically opposed' but must comply from 1/1/2027, and CAT surge capacity is the pain. (2) Sampling-design defensibility. The fight is over how many samples, where, and against what background, and no independent tool scores a sampling plan or existing IH report for adequacy, though this is what class actions and the Purdue review turn on. (3) A neutral, versioned crosswalk from AIHA/IICRC/40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels and 8 CCR 1529 asbestos to a per-home plan, which updates when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. (4) Pooled, structured sampling data across claims, which is what regulators reuse. EFRU holds only a few dozen homes.

Two facts weaken the 'vacuum' framing. Interim lead and asbestos thresholds already exist in AB 1642 (40 CFR 745.227(e)(8)(viii) and 8 CCR 1529). The vacuum is mainly sampling design and non-lead contaminants such as cyanide, other metals and dioxins.

Structural risks: the buyer conflict, because carriers may not adopt a protocol seen as policyholder-friendly and policyholder-side buyers want a testifying CIH rather than software. Remote IH sign-off and technician-collected samples may run into CIH and certification expectations. Any advantage is capped at the moment DTSC publishes standards.

Research limits: my web-search budget ran out before I could run Crunchbase, YC and TechCrunch-specific queries. The general startup searches (wildfire smoke assessment startup, chain-of-custody kits, technician network) found only wildfire-detection companies (Pano AI, FireScan, FireSafe AI), none in post-fire smoke-damage assessment. Treat 'no funded startup' as probable, not proven.
evidence_of_demand:
Demand is strong and forced by law, but the paying buyer is not the one the idea assumes.

Statute: AB 1795 (signed 9/15/2026, effective 1/1/2027) makes insurers inspect within 30 days and pay for sampling and testing needed to restore homes to pre-loss condition and clear them for occupancy (Sec. 2060.2(b), (d)(1)). It sets a rebuttable presumption that smoke, ash, soot and char in a surviving home in the impact zone came from the fire, and bars ALE termination before clearance (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1795 ; https://www.insurancebusinessmag.com/us/news/property/california-sets-first-wildfire-smoke-testing-rules-for-insurers-588314.aspx). DTSC standards are due end-2028 (lead and asbestos) and end-2029 (other contaminants) (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260ab1642 ; https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/california-los-angeles-palisades-eaton-fires-smoke-damage-bills-signed-wildfire-insurance). CalMatters/Pleasanton Weekly describe a gap of about 2+ years (https://www.pleasantonweekly.com/calmatters/2026/09/15/new-california-law-sets-first-in-nation-standards-for-smoke-damage-in-homes/).

Volume: coverage of the CDI task force cites more than 42,000 LA-fire claims from Jan-Nov 2025, over 13,000 of them standing homes with smoke damage. I could not pin the exact source. CDI task force report (3/9/2026): https://www.insurance.ca.gov/01-consumers/140-catastrophes/Smoke-Claims-Remediation-Report.cfm

Litigation over sampling design: Ghazarian v. Fire Insurance Exchange and HygieneTech class action (https://pasadenanow.com/main/altadena-homeowners-sue-farmers-insurance-testing-firm-over-eaton-fire-smoke-claims); a second class action against a carrier and its hygiene vendor (https://www.law.com/therecorder/2026/02/27/hygiene-companies-face-class-actions-over-alleged-failure-to-properly-test-homes-for-toxins-after-eaton-wildfire-/); LA County suit vs State Farm, 8/31/2026 (https://www.liveinsurancenews.com/smoke-damage-claims-california/8575801/).

The problem the idea names, thin sampling: carrier-retained hygienists take about ten samples in a 3,000 sq ft home (1 per 300 sq ft), skip wall cavities, attic insulation and HVAC unless the homeowner pays, and cap budgets in advance (https://www.propertyinsurancecoveragelaw.com/blog/california-wildfire-smoke-claims/). Purdue reports consultants using improper methods and incorrect comparison standards (https://engineering.purdue.edu/PlumbingSafety/resources/wildfire-response).

Willingness to pay: independent testing runs $2,000-$20,000+ (https://www.kerleyschaffer.com/blog/fair-plan-hygenist-testing-guide). Homeowners already pay about $2k-$4k out of pocket, which supports the $1,800-$4,500 price point. EFRU's data on about 50 remediated homes showed 63% with elevated lead and one third with asbestos (https://laist.com/news/housing-homelessness/altadena-eaton-fire-homes-post-remediation-testing-lead-asbestos).

Not found: any carrier, TPA or RFP saying it wants to buy a third-party protocol or compliance dashboard. Carriers oppose the bills and retain their own vendors (https://calmatters.org/economy/2026/09/smoke-damage-insurance-bills/). The claimed $2-$5 per claim per month SaaS demand is unvalidated.
sharper_angle:
Drop 'write the standard' and the 'training and certification' revenue line. Build the AB 1795 defensibility and compliance layer as a capital-light, software-first product.

1. Sell a sampling-plan generator and adequacy auditor to carriers, TPAs and litigation-side buyers. The plan generator sets zone-aware sample counts and locations, including attics, HVAC and wall cavities, and picks the comparison basis: EPA 40 CFR 745.227 lead-dust levels, 8 CCR 1529 asbestos, and pre-/post-remediation and background controls. Every plan cites AIHA, IICRC/RIA/CIRI and Purdue and is versioned so it re-maps when DTSC issues standards in 2028-29. The auditor scores any existing IH report against the same grid, which is the exact issue in the HygieneTech and State Farm actions. That serves the 'fight is the sampling design' insight without a technician army.

2. Use existing CIH and IICRC firms as the labor pool and operate as the compliance and evidence layer: 30-day clock, chain-of-custody, lab results, audit trail. Rimkus, EHS, Safeguard and similar firms are then partners or channel, not enemies. Sign remote CIH-of-record through partner firms rather than hiring your own, to avoid licensure and certification exposure.

3. Take a neutral-standards posture: an advisory board of CIHs plus a toxicologist, public methodology, and an anonymized cross-claim dataset. Aim to be the data source DTSC and CDI can cite. Try to get pilot data-sharing with EFRU and Purdue instead of competing with their free guides.

4. Start with the buyers who feel the pain and can be reached before 1/1/2027, and validate before building. The first test is whether one carrier or TPA claims team will pay for a paid pilot on 10-20 files. Public adjusters and policyholder attorneys are the fastest early revenue (expert-evidence sampling plans and report audits). Use the subsidized pilot assessments only as data collection. If no carrier or TPA will sign, the fallback is a PA and attorney tool.

5. Position for the next fire. AB 1795 covers any declared wildfire, and other states (CO, OR, HI) will copy California. A product that re-maps to whichever standard governs is more durable than a California-specific interim protocol that dies in 2028.

Before committing, verify the chaptered AB 1795 text on three points: interim local-agency standards, the state training and certification programs, and any qualified-person requirements for samplers. One source (Insurance Business) says DTSC emergency regulations are due 7/1/2027 and that AIHA and IICRC guides 'carry statutory force'. CalMatters, LAist and the AB 1642 text say end-2028 and end-2029, and I did not find the statutory-force claim in the bill text I could read.
